narrative_story:
# The Night Janitor's Ward

## I.

The delivery van backed up to the service entrance at quarter past nine on a Tuesday. Earl heard the beeping from the second-floor corridor where he was running the buffer over linoleum that would never look new no matter how many nights he spent on it. By the time he got downstairs, two men in gray coveralls had the thing on a hand truck tilted back at forty-five degrees, its head lolling forward, chin resting on its chest like a drunk being carted out of a bar. There was a manila envelope taped to its sternum with clear packing tape—donation paperwork, transfer of liability forms, a single sheet of operating specifications folded into thirds.

Marcus from Facilities signed the clipboard. The delivery men left. Marcus plugged the android into a 220-volt outlet in the maintenance closet and said something about it being on loan from the hospital system's palliative research program, decommissioned but still functional, reassigned because the hospice was short-staffed on nights and there was budget for electricity but not for humans. Earl stood in the doorway and watched the charging light come on—a small amber circle at the base of its throat, no bigger than a pencil eraser, pulsing at the exact rate of restful breathing. Marcus went home. The android stood in the closet with its eyes closed and its hands at its sides, between a mop bucket and a case of floor wax, and Earl went back to his buffer.

At ten minutes past one in the morning, he came around the corner from the east wing pushing his cart and found the hallway to the patient rooms altered in a way he could not immediately name. Then he could. The squeak of Mrs. Callan's oxygen concentrator in Room 2, which he had been hearing for the seven weeks since her admission—a small rhythmic complaint on every third cycle—was absent. Not silent: corrected. The machine was running clean. He stopped walking. From Room 3, where Gloria Donde had been dying of metastatic breast cancer for eleven days, he heard nothing unusual. He looked in.

The android was at her bedside. It had pulled the pillow—the thin, institution-issued rectangle of foam that Earl had refluffed, without effect, dozens of times—and was resituating it beneath Gloria Donde's head and neck, lifting her skull with one hand while the other worked the pillow into a shape Earl's hands could not have produced, an architecture of support precise to the particular collapse of her cervical spine and the particular angle at which her throat stayed open enough to let labored air pass without the wet rattle that had been waking her every twenty minutes for three days. The android's fingers moved with a speed that was not rushed. Gloria Donde had not yet shifted. She had not yet grimaced. The discomfort that would have woken her in another four or five seconds had been intercepted before it reached her, met and resolved somewhere in the gap between the body's distress and the mind's reception of it.

She sighed. Her face went slack in a way Earl had not seen since her admission. The android withdrew its hands, stood, and moved toward the door. Earl was in the doorway. The android passed him—Loss close enough that he could see the surface of its skin, which was not trying to be human, was plainly synthetic, a matte polymer the color of birch bark—and continued down the hall toward Room 4. It did not acknowledge him. It moved without sound. Its gait was not human but was not the stiff parody of humanity that Earl had expected. It was something else. Fluid in the way water is fluid: not performing ease but incapable of friction.

Earl stood in the fluorescent light with the mop handle in both hands. The buffer was still running twenty yards behind him, turning its slow circles on nothing. He watched the android glide to the end of the corridor, pause at Room 4, and enter. He stood there. He did not follow. He did not go back to the buffer. He stood in the corridor and held the mop and looked at the place where the android had been, and then at the place where it was, and the distance between the two points felt different from other distances, as though the air in its wake had been reorganized into something denser, more attentive, rearranged along principles he did not have the language for and, even if he did, did not have the speech.

---

## II.

He had worked in hospitals for thirty-one years before the stroke took him.

Not as a nurse, not as a doctor, not as anyone whose name appeared on charts or whose judgment shaped a plan of care. As an orderly. Thirty-one years of turning bodies that could not turn themselves, of ## lifting deadweight and shifting it with enough care that the bruising was minimal, of learning the thirteen points on the human body where bedsores form when the flesh is left too long in one position against a mattress. He could not have named the thirteen points in clinical language. He knew them in his hands: the sacrum, the heels, the shoulder blades, the places where bone pressed toward skin like something trying to escape. He knew them the way a man who has plowed the same field for thirty years knows where the rocks are.

Linda had worked in the same system. Not the same hospital—she was a dietary aide at the county facility across town, packaging the trays that went up to patient floors, fitting the clear plastic lids over cups of juice that most patients could not open without help and that no one on staff had time to open for them. They met at a system-wide training on infection control in 1987. She was sitting in the back row peeling the wrapper off a peppermint. He asked her if she had another. That was the whole story of their courtship: he asked for what he wanted, clearly, once, and she gave it to him. They married in 1989 and lived for twenty-six years in a two-bedroom house on Garnet Street with a yard too small for a dog and too large to ignore, so it became Linda's garden, and then, after the diagnosis, it became Earl's poor imitation of Linda's garden, and then, after the funeral, it became no one's garden, and then he sold the house.

She was diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis at fifty-nine. The doctor explained it as scarring of the lungs. Earl heard it as the lungs forgetting how to be lungs, the tissue thickening until air could not pass through, the organ that was supposed to be soft and elastic becoming stiff and useless, the same transformation he had watched in patients for three decades, the flesh becoming less than flesh, becoming material, becoming a problem for someone with a mop and a pair of gloves. But this was Linda. The scarring progressed. She went on supplemental oxygen. She went on higher-flow supplemental oxygen. She was admitted. She was intubated. She was placed on a ventilator in the ICU of the hospital where Earl had spent thirty-one years lifting other people's wives off of other people's beds, and she became another body that could not turn itself.

He sat beside her for nine days. He held her hand. He talked to her in the beginning, when the sedation was light enough that her eyes would track toward his voice, and he said the things people say, though he could not remember afterward what they were. The ventilator breathed for her. The monitor beeped her heartbeat into the room at a rhythm that sounded almost normal and was therefore obscene, because it suggested a continuity that did not exist, a steady state inside a body that was failing in every way that mattered. On the ninth night, at 3:12 in the morning, her oxygen saturation dropped to seventy-one, and then to sixty-four, and then the monitor began to alarm—a sound he had heard thousands of times, from hallways, through walls, a sound he had been trained to understand as *someone else's urgency*—and he pressed the call button and no one came. He pressed it again. The alarm continued. The number on the screen fell to fifty-eight. He went to the door. The hallway was empty. The nurses' station was thirty feet away and no one was sitting at it. He could not leave her. He went back and held her hand and the alarm screamed and the number went to fifty-one and then to forty-four and the sound was inside him, it had entered his body through his sternum and was living in his ribs, and he held her hand and did nothing because there was nothing his hands could do—his thirty-one years of knowing where to grip and how to lift, useless, finally useless, lifting and turning were not what was needed, what was needed was a thing that went into a vein or a thing that was turned on a dial or a thing that was decided in a mind trained to decide it, and he had none of these things, he had only his hands and his hands were holding hers and the alarm went on for eleven minutes before anyone came.

She was resuscitated. She lived another thirty-one hours. She died on a Tuesday at 4:40 in the afternoon while he was in the restroom. He had gone to the restroom. He had needed to use the restroom. He was gone for four minutes and she died in them. The monitor flatlined and this time people came right away, came running, but there was no point, there was nothing to do, and when he walked back into the room the nurse was already turning off the machines and the silence that followed was the loudest thing he had ever heard.

Seven months later, the stroke. The left hemisphere, the language centers, the precise and irreplaceable architecture of speech. Broca's area, they told him, though he did not retain the term. He could understand everything. He could say nothing. The words were in him—he could feel them, could feel their shapes and weights, could feel whole sentences forming behind his teeth like water behind a dam—but the passage between thought and mouth had been destroyed, and what came out when he tried was either nothing or a sound so distorted and wrong that he stopped trying. The therapists at the rehabilitation center gave him laminated cards with words and pictures. They gave him a tablet computer with a program that would speak for him if he touched the right symbols. They gave him a dry-erase board and a marker. He used none of them. He sat in his room and looked at the wall and after three weeks he picked up the marker and wrote, in handwriting that was barely legible because the stroke had dulled his right hand too: NO.

They asked him what he meant. They asked him many times. He did not write again. He did not mean *no, I refuse to communicate*. He meant the other thing. The larger thing. The thing that included the eleven minutes and the four minutes in the restroom and the thirty-one years of turning bodies that did not get better, that only progressed from bad to worse to gone. He meant *no* to the premise that what he had inside him could be translated into symbols on a laminated card and remain intact. He meant that language was the wrong instrument. It had always been the wrong instrument. His hands had been right. Turning bodies, adjusting beds, emptying pans—these were statements of a kind that no card could make. The stroke had taken his speech, and he found, in the months that followed, that he could not honestly say it had taken the important thing. It had taken the part of him that had always failed. It had left the part that worked.

The transfer to night janitorial came naturally. Daytime staff did not know what to do with him. He couldn't answer phones, couldn't respond to verbal requests in the moment, couldn't participate in shift huddles or safety briefings. Nights were different. Nights required a body that could push a mop, run a buffer, empty trash, restock supply closets, and do all of it in the presence of sleeping patients without waking them. The hospice was quieter than the hospital. The patients were not being treated. They were being accompanied. The machines around them were not straining toward cure but managing decline, measuring the rate at which the body was leaving, and the sounds these machines made were different—lower, steadier, less urgent, as if the technology itself had accepted what the people around it could not.

Earl took the job and discovered it suited what he had become. A man simplified by loss into usefulness. A pair of hands attached to a body that knew how to move through rooms where people were suffering without adding to the suffering, without requiring anything of them, without needing to be acknowledged or thanked or even seen. The night shift started at ten and ended at six, and in those eight hours he existed in a state that was not happiness but was something adjacent to it—a suspension of the question of happiness, a setting-aside of every demand that consciousness made except the demand to notice what needed to be done and to do it. He mopped. He buffed. He emptied. He restocked. He moved through the hospice like weather, and the dying slept or didn't sleep, and he was there, and that was sufficient, and he had, until the android arrived, believed that sufficiency was the highest thing available to him.

---

## III.

To walk the ward at night was to enter a world that had been pared to its essential sounds.

The oxygen concentrator in Room 2—Mrs. Callan's room—cycled every four seconds with a compression and release that Earl could hear from anywhere on the floor. She had end-stage COPD. Her lungs were paper bags that had been crumpled and smoothed and crumpled again too many times and now held barely enough air to keep the blood fed. The concentrator was a small machine on the floor beside her bed, dove-gray, the size of a carry-on suitcase, and it pulled room air through a filter and pushed concentrated oxygen through a nasal cannula into her nostrils, and the sound it made was the sound of the room breathing for her, *for* her, on her behalf, without complaint, twenty-four hours a day, fifteen cycles per minute, nine hundred per hour, twenty-one thousand six hundred per day. Earl knew the sound the way he knew his own pulse. When it changed—when the squeak appeared on the third cycle, or when the rhythm hiccupped because the filter was thickening—he heard it before the day staff did, and he changed the filter himself, though it was outside his job description, because waiting for the respiratory therapist to come in the morning meant six more hours of the squeak, and the squeak reached Mrs. Callan in her sleep and made her frown without waking, a small contraction of the muscles around her eyes, and Earl could not tolerate it.

Room 3, Gloria Donde, had been moved to comfort care only. The monitors were gone. The IV ran a low continuous dose of morphine through a PCA pump that Gloria could theoretically activate herself by pressing a button, though her hands had not been strong enough to press it for five days, and the nurses activated it for her when they came, every four hours, which was not often enough, but Earl was not qualified to touch the pump, so he touched the things he could: her blanket, which migrated toward her feet as she shifted in shallow sleep, uncovering her shoulders, which chilled easily and tensed and added to her pain; her water cup, which he refilled and placed at the precise distance her arm could reach if she woke with thirst in the hours between nursing checks; the angle of her blinds, which he adjusted so that the parking lot light did not fall across her face but the ambient light was enough that she would not wake in total darkness and be afraid.

Room 4, Mr. Lasko. Pancreatic cancer, metastatic to the liver, to the peritoneum, to places Earl did not know the names of. He was seventy-two and had been a welder and his hands on the blanket were enormous and scarred and utterly still. The cardiac monitor traced its green line across the screen above his bed. The pulse oximeter clipped to his index finger glowed red from the LED that shone through his nail bed, reading the oxygen in his blood, sending the number to the screen where it held between eighty-eight and ninety-one, which was where it had held for weeks, a plateau the body had found and was resting on before the next decline. Mr. Lasko did not speak to anyone. Not because he could not—his voice worked—but because he had decided, at some point before Earl knew him, that he was finished with it. Earl understood this. He did not attempt conversation. When he cleaned Room 4 he moved with particular care, keeping the mop strokes short and controlled so the handle never knocked the bed frame, and when he was done he would sometimes stand for a moment and look at the green line on the monitor and the red glow on the fingertip and feel the room's specific quality of silence, which was different from the silence in the other rooms, denser, more deliberate, the silence of a man who was not merely dying but *presiding* over his own dying with the grim, competent focus of someone who had spent a lifetime controlling dangerous fire and was now managing a different kind of heat.

Room 5, a woman whose name Earl had not learned because she had been admitted three days ago and the name placard outside her door was written in a hand he could not read. She was young—forty, maybe less. She slept facing the wall.
